They put it back the next day, in secret, while the company marched: the journal to its hidden sleeve, the letter to its place among the later pages. She never knew it had been gone. I will leave it to my readers to decide whether that was kindness or merely good tactics. In this company it is often hard to tell the two apart, and I have stopped trying.

IV. The Gateway to Chult

Three more days of green. Three more nights of the dome and the watches and the forest's dripping clock. Then on the twenty-fourth of Uktar the trees fell away and the land went down northward to the sea, and there was Port Nyanzaru.

I have written of it before, and I will write of it again, because no city in the Realms repays the pen like this one. It climbs its hills in colors a Waterdhavian would call indecent: ochre and saffron and a blue the sky itself envies, roofs of red tile glittering with the last rain, the great domes of the Merchants' Ward catching the afternoon light. Beneath the colors the streets run with cart-dinosaurs and hawkers and the smell of frying plantain and the deeper, meatier smell that gives the Red Bazaar its name. Out in the bay, on its rock, the Temple of Sune stood with its mirrored walls making its roof seem to hang in the air, which is exactly the sort of thing Sune's people would do, and which I have always rather admired.

The company did what adventurers do in cities. They shopped, and what a company buys tells you what it expects. A shield for Chumble Crudluck. Chain and iron spikes, a net, a ten-foot pole, caltrops and ball bearings to scatter behind them, which together say we expect to be chased. And potions of healing, eight of them, which say we expect to be hit.

And Shago was paid. His wages had been owed since the gladiator first signed on with them at Fort Beluarian and were long in arrears, and a guide who has killed for you at Hrakhamar and in the ruins of Mbala, and stood beside you with a death-writ on his own head, has earned his coin. It pleased me to hear that it was counted out in full.

Then, with Nerissa left in the keeping of Artus and Dragonbait, who could be trusted not to lose her, the five went south from the Red Bazaar into the Market Ward, to an inn.

V. Kaya's House of Repose

A word about the house. Kaya's is one of the more prosperous inns of the Market Ward, built for travelers who want their comfort with a little gilt on it, and I give it four tankards out of five, docking one only because the house charges Waterdeep prices for Chultan rum and knows it. The common room is wide and lamplit, with a dartboard on the back wall that has seen more blood than some battlefields.

The man they wanted was not there when they arrived. He came later, when the lamps were lit and the room was full: a loose, friendly, red-faced fellow who sat with his back to the corner and a glass at his elbow and a handwritten book open on the table before him, and who gave off the air of a man who had been drunk in that chair so many evenings that the chair had begun to take his shape. Soggy Wren. A ranking agent of the Harpers, if you can credit it, and once, in his youth, a sorcerer of real promise, before he discovered that there was a thirst he liked better than the thirst for power.

The company did not approach him. They sent the pickle.

Wickles, Chumble's familiar, drifted invisible over the man's shoulder and read his book as he read it, and reported back what he saw. A name, Diammsar, written down as a traitor. Sketches of the Temple of Sune, the mirrored temple on its rock, with stick figures marking where the temple's people stood and where the ones doing the business would move among them, several of the figures drawn, in the manner of their draughtsman, rather more anatomically than any plan required. Notes toward that business, to be done by a goliath, a dwarf, a human, and a tiefling.

The company knew that roster. They had seen it at an inn in this very city two months before: the shield dwarf, the goliath ranger, the human cleric, and the tiefling wizard who had hired away Musharib, their own first guide in Chult, and gone off to find the Soulmonger by way of Kitcher's Inlet. Whatever Soggy Wren was running, Musharib's new employers had been running it for him.

Then Grieg and Lilac Mist went to the dartboard.

They played badly, on purpose, which for a wulven hunter and a tabaxi ranger is harder than playing well, and on her turn Lilac Mist let a dart go wide, wide enough that it carried her across the room to retrieve it from the vicinity of the red-faced man's table. It was as unsubtle an approach as I have ever recorded, and it worked perfectly, because Soggy Wren is a man who has never in his life let a stranger pass within arm's length without offering them a drink. He suggested one at once. The company accepted at once. And the questioning began.

I will say that it was not gentle. These five have been long enough in Chult to have learned that time is the one thing the Death Curse does not give back, and they came at Wren hard, all of them at once, with the whole weight of what they knew. They told him they had been hunting the curse since Waterdeep. They told him they had found Omu, the lost city under the canopy where the Soulmonger sits. They told him they meant to kill Ras Nsi. Wren wrote it all down in his book as they said it, his pen moving a little behind his glass, and the company watched him realize two things at once: that they were not people he could get rid of, and that they had just handed him more about the Death Curse than his own investigation had turned up in a month.

So he opened up. Drink makes some men liars and some men honest, and Wren is the second kind.

Chumble Crudluck raised a hand and shaped the air above the table, and a minor image stood there a moment in the lamplight: a tall dark woman with green eyes, in the gear of a city that no longer stood. Wren knew her before the goblin had finished. Mesika, he said: a good woman who had been helping him look into the curse.

Then he told them about the amulet. It had come into Port Nyanzaru in pieces, smuggled by the yuan-ti, and the Harpers and their friends in the Ytepka Society had gathered the pieces as they surfaced. One piece Musharib's company had lifted for him in a quiet operation inside the Temple of Sune. Another had been won, of all things, in a dinosaur race. (Here the reader will think of the wager ticket in the hidden sleeve, as I did when the tale reached me, and as I am certain the gnome did at the table.) Wren's people had chased the thing because they took it for a piece of the Death Curse, and the longer they looked the clearer it became that it was not. It was something else. Something the yuan-ti had made for a purpose of their own.

He put it on the table.

Urida laid her hands near it and spoke the words of identification, and the room went quiet around her the way rooms do around a wizard at work, and when she looked up she had it.

The amulet is a dreamer's tool. Set near a sleeping person, night after night, it works on them while they sleep, turning their sympathies by slow degrees toward the yuan-ti, until they wake one morning a friend to the serpent folk without ever having chosen to be. It does not work on just anyone. It is tuned, like a sending stone, to a single soul.

It was tuned to Jessamine.

Readers who have followed this chronicle will feel the floor shift as the company did. Jessamine, who sits among the seven merchant princes and casts the deciding vote when they are divided. Jessamine, who deals in plants and poison and sanctioned death, who hides her rotting flesh beneath black bandages because the Soulmonger's curse is eating her alive, and who, for exactly that reason, has twice now looked kindly on this company and their purpose. The yuan-ti had built a key for her sleeping mind. What they wanted with a merchant prince's vote, neither the company nor I can tell you; Wren's own letter had it that the amulet was no part of the Death Curse, and nothing the company has learned ties the serpent folk to it. But this is the same city where a yuan-ti pureblood was seen slipping away from a rooftop on the day a water barrel nearly killed Urida, and the company stopped taking the serpent folk's interest in Port Nyanzaru for coincidence a long time ago.

They had not managed it. The pieces had scattered, the Harpers had gathered them, and the thing now lay on a tavern table under a gnome's hands instead of under a merchant prince's pillow. But it had been meant, and in Chult what is meant once is generally meant again.

VI. What Remains

So the company came out of Kaya's House of Repose into the warm night with more than they went in with, as this company generally does.

They went in for a drunken Harper and came out with the name of the woman sleeping in Artus Cimber's camp: not Nerissa, but Mesika, warrior of Mezro, who a month ago was walking the streets of this city with a notebook and a wager ticket, investigating the Death Curse beside a man who could barely stand, and who ten days ago was struck by a fire of every color and woke believing she had just come from a patrol outside walls that fell a hundred years before. Her journal learns the same things over and over. Her mind is a dropped pot. And she is the last thread in all Chult that leads back to the lost city and the woman Artus has spent his life walking toward.

They mean to tell him. I would not care to be in the room.

Then they mean to go south again, back to the Halls between the rivers, to collect Xhosala from her reclaimed temple and go on south with her toward the Forsaken Tree, fifty miles further south between the Tiryki and the Olung, in blighted country where the dead walk in daylight: a darkwood trunk that rises above the canopy on the very spot where a priestess and a thief destroyed each other a century ago, and under whose roots a corrupted god's heart lies waiting in a coin.

They are better provisioned for it than they were. Eight potions. A ten-foot pole. A bag of ball bearings.

I have written of a great many heroes, and I have learned to distrust the ones who never turn back. This company turned back. They went home for potions and paid their guide and read a sleeping woman's diary and bought a drunk a drink, and in doing so they learned more in five days than most companies learn in a season. That is not the stuff of ballads. It is the stuff of victories.

Mark the name Mesika. And mark, if you are the marking kind, that the serpent folk wanted a merchant prince's dreams, and did not get them, and is unlikely to have stopped wanting.

V.G.

title: What Waits Below
summary:
The Tiryki Anchorage lies outside Port Nyanzaru's southeastern wall, where the Tiryki fans out into its delta and gives itself up to the Bay of Chult, and the city's laws give themselves up with it. It is cheap rooms and unregulated docks, dinosaur pens that can be smelled from the Red Bazaar on even a moderately warm evening, and the sort of lodging a man takes when he has reasons not to be found. Artus Cimber keeps an apartment there. Of course he does.

The company came to it from Kaya's House of Repose with the lamps already lit in the twilight of the evening, and found the three of them inside: Artus, the saurial, and the woman who called herself Nerissa, talking over the company's recent travels. It was an easy scene to walk into and a hard one to disrupt without a loss of proper decorum. The company needed to speak with Artus in private, and so they tried to be as subtle as they could.

Vex and Urida went in. The other three stayed in the hall. The dragonborn caught Artus's eye across the room with the smallest motion of his head, and when the man came over, Vex spoke to him in Draconic, low and brief, saying only that there was something to discuss, privately. Artus nodded, in spite of the questions running through his mind, and motioned the group to a back room, as the gnome settled herself on the couch beside the woman from Mezro to be company for her and for Dragonbait, or, more so, to distract from any eyes that might follow the parade heading into the other room.

Behind the door, the company laid it out. Her name is Mesika. She had been living in Port Nyanzaru for at least a few weeks, helping a Harper named Wren look into the Death Curse. There was a letter. There was a wager ticket from the dinosaur races. There was a journal in her own hand. All three pointed decidedly at this fact. They did not stop there, and I give them credit for it, because the next step was the unkind one. A month in Port Nyanzaru does not fit a woman who, ten days before they met her, was by her own account standing guard outside a living Mezro. Perhaps she had never been there at all. Perhaps none of it was true.

Artus sat with it a moment, as a man does who has been handed a great deal at once. "The Harpers," he said. "Good to know they are finally doing something, at least." That she had borrowed the name Nerissa did not surprise him in the least, as he had mentioned a similar theory a few days before. Mesika was a name unfamiliar to his ear, though he was quick to add that he had not been to Mezro in a very long time. It was the last part he would not follow them into, however. Artus Cimber has been hunted for longer than most men live, and a man like that learns to doubt a stranger's story as a matter of habit. He could not doubt this one. "She knows things about that city that no one who was not there could know," he said. "You do not find such things in a library. Mezro has been gone a hundred years, as far as the world knows, and there is no one left alive who could tell her how its last days went." Could she be inventing it? "Perhaps," he allowed. "Hard to say. But I really cannot see it."

He then paused, and asked the question that mattered to him most, trying desperately to not let it sound that way. "Forgive me if this sounds self-absorbed," he said, "but did you happen to speak of me with this Harper?"

They had not. They had told Wren what they knew of the Death Curse, and that were they to fail, there would be someone else working toward resolving it, and they had left the someone unnamed. Artus was visibly relieved, and he explained the relief. "The rank and file of the Harpers are decent people, for the most part. Those who lead them are another matter. And I have been given to understand that they may be looking for me as well. That my name is on a list of theirs, of people to be hunted down." Best, then, if they did not know he was in the city. "Or at the least, that they not know it for certain."

Back to the true matter at hand, that of the enigmatic Mesika. What was to be done about her? Perhaps there was some magical entity controlling her, a possession, a mystical working of some kind. If only one could look inside her mind and see the truth of it. All eyes went to the man with the ring. He shook his head. "I have dealt with a great deal of magic in my time, but I am no wizard. I cannot read minds. The ring does many things, but its powers are not infinite." His counsel was simpler than magic: tell her the name, and watch what it does to her.

So they went back out, and they did.

I want to be fair to this company about how they did it, because they could have done it tactlessly and did not. They did not accuse. They did not spring the journal on her. They stood in a loose ring around her where she sat, five of them and Artus behind, and asked her, gently, to help them understand the facts that had come to light that day. And the woman from Mezro, who in three tendays of acquaintance had never once looked anything but a soldier, began to answer in starts and stops, like someone searching a dark room for a thing she had put down somewhere.

The light had come first. "I remember the light," she told them. "Every color at once, like a blue flame, and it covered me. I remember reaching out to it. Touching it. I cannot tell you why I would do such a thing, but I remember doing it, and then I was standing in water. In the drowned ruin of the city, with the dead all around me, ancient and dried to leather." Did Port Nyanzaru look familiar to her? "I am not sure of anything any longer. None of it is familiar to me. But I no longer trust what is familiar and what is not."

Wren? She looked lost in thought a moment. "Perhaps. There is something in it." When they told her that he knew her, that he had seen her in the city for weeks, something in her shifted toward fear. "Knows me how? What did he say of me?"

And then they gave her the name.

She went still. Then she began to tremble, and I am told it was the first crack any of them had seen in her. "I could not remember my name," she said. "I saw Nerissa on a notice as I walked into town, and I took it. I could not bring myself to tell anyone that I did not know my own." And then, slower, after pulling in a deep breath: "Mesika is more familiar. That is more like me. That feels right." She said it again, quietly to herself, several times, the way one tests a step on a stair.

Then the arithmetic reached her. "Then there are weeks I cannot account for," she said. "What did I do in them? Did I hurt anyone?" They told her the truth as they knew it: she had wagered on dinosaur races as part of a mission to help an investigation into the curse, and had run errands in the city's defense. "Then I tried to help people. That is something. That is good to know." A pause. "Did I succeed?" On one, they thought, she had. She took that in. And then, haltingly, she gave them the confession underneath the confession. "It shamed me, when I met you, how much I could not remember. So I held to the visions, because they had led me to you, and I put the gaps out of my mind, all the things a soldier of Mezro ought to know and I did not. I never meant to deceive you. You must believe that. I did not want to be taken for a madwoman." She had needed to stay with them, she said, because she had been led to that hall for a reason, and the reason was them.

Grieg was watching her as she said it, and a wulven's eyes miss less than his manner suggests. What he saw was a woman thoroughly shaken, in a panic, but not the panic of the caught. It was the panic of someone who cannot believe this is happening to her. She believed every word she was saying. He has seldom been so sure of anything.

"The vision that showed me you in the temple was not the only one," she went on. "There have been others since. Flashes. People and places, and I do not know them. But each one leaves me understanding a little more, as though something were leading me back toward remembering, a step at a time." When she tried to think back to the temple, it was as though everything then had rushed past her faster than she could take it in. "It is slower now. Things are filling in."

They asked her for her pack, and showed her the hidden flap Urida had found. "I never saw that was there," she said. "What is it?" She opened the journal and went pale, and read a page. "That is my writing. I know my own hand." And then, more quietly: "Thank you for bringing this to me. You might simply have cast me out."

Then they told her she would not be coming to Omu. Artus wanted her safe, for what she was to Mezro, and where they were going was no place for anyone they wished to keep safe. She protested as a soldier protests. "I can still fight. I can help with what the Obanashi need of you. I can help you with this Forsaken Tree." And when that did not move them: "And you tell me Ras Nsi lives. The enemy of all Mezro. Surely his throat deserves my blades." They let the protest stand. The matter of Omu was not for that night.

Asked what year it was, she gave the answer this whole chronicle has been circling since she first walked into the temple at the Seething Halls. "I would have told you it was 1385. I know now that it is not. I saw Mezro in ruins with my own eyes, and it had the look of a place long dead." Whatever had happened to her had somehow carried the years past her, and she could not understand it. "I am no wizard. I know nothing of such things."

Dragonbait, through all of it, gave off honeysuckle and roses with the lightest touch of ham. Artus watched with a face the company read as interest and sadness in equal measure, and when it had gone on long enough, he was the one who said to let it all sink in overnight.

They slept at his place. In the morning, she was Mesika, and nobody called her anything else again.

They set out the following morn, overland. Before they left, Lilac Mist settled Mr. Stompy at the Tiryki Anchorage pens, where her name is known to the racing crowds: free room and board, on the condition that he stand at stud while she was away. I am given to understand he accepted the terms.

Four days later, they came to the Seething Halls, entering by the now-familiar tunnel in the mountain's flank through which they had first come. There was no other choice, as the main door is still a slope of fallen stone that six people with hand tools cannot shift. Xhosala met them inside and told them they were right on time. Her people had cleared what could be cleared, and the rest would wait for stoneworkers. They were ready.

On the first night out, with Artus, Dragonbait, Vex, and Chumble Crudluck at the fire, the pickle heard fighting past the edge of the camp. Wickles hears a great deal, for a vegetable. He went to look, invisible and unhurried, and came back to report: Xhosala's people, finishing off a handful of zombies with blue triangles on their foreheads. A few minutes later Xhosala threw one of the heads down beside the fire. "Ran into some of the triangle lads out there," she said. "Deep enough in the jungle, you see them. Not all of them. But enough."

Readers of this chronicle will remember a mark like it, painted on the brows of cannibals months ago. Artus Cimber looked at the head by the fire and knew this one for something older. "In Mezro that was the mark of the exile and the prisoner," he said. "Ras Nsi took it for his own. He used it to brand his army of the dead." Xhosala poked the head with her foot. "Well. These, at least, are no longer anyone's concern."

Across the Tiryki, the jungle changed. Xhosala's people took the point now, since they knew the ground, and the company fell in behind in their marching order, with Grieg and Shago, who ordinarily walk at the front and see first, somewhere in the middle of a longer column than they were used to. I mention this because of what came of it.

It was midday on the Feast of the Moon, the day Faerûn sets aside to remember its dead, when the Obanashi hunters began to fan out ahead, circling something, and one of the acolytes turned to point. Ninety feet off through the trees, fading in and out between the trunks, a figure was coming toward them, and around it hung a cloud. Not mist. Something darker and busier, that moved as the figure moved. And the figure moved with purpose. Not the stagger of a zombie or the rattle of a skeleton: the gait of a thing that knew where it was going.

Xhosala's archers had already put arrows into it, but it seemed to pay the piercing shots no mind, continuing its pace. The company could have let the mage hunters handle it. They waved the mage hunters off instead, and went in.

Lilac Mist opened. Her mark settled on the thing and two arrows followed it in, and I am told the second of them alone would have brought down a lesser creature; together they did a day's damage in a breath. Chumble's eldritch blasts hammered after them. Urida's fire bolt came in on the heels of the blasts. The thing was barely standing before it had taken a step toward them.

Then the cloud split.

It split into two clouds, and the clouds split into things, and the things were stirges: bat-sized, bloated, needle-mouthed horrors that are half bat and half mosquito, with pincer legs to hold on by (my own Guide has them, and I will say the illustration does not do justice to the sound). They had been feeding on the walking corpse. Now they had smelled something warmer. They came at the living from every side, at the mage hunters and the company alike, and Grieg, who had not seen them coming, had two of them on him before he could get his trident up. They hit him hard, through armor that very little hits, and the proboscises went in, and the stirges hung there off him like leeches off a hound and began to drink.

He did not panic. He got the tines of the trident in under the first one, pried it off his own body and stabbed it into the ground, and it burst. His echo stepped out of him, that translucent shade of himself the wulven sends ahead into trouble, and between the two of them the second stirge came apart the same way. Vex cut his out of the air with one stroke of the scimitar and found that the thing was dead before the stroke was finished. A stirge, it turns out, is a bag of someone else's blood with wings on it. Hit one and it pops in a horrifically gory explosion.

The wight reached the nearest living thing it could, and that was Zamisi, one of Xhosala's scouts. It swung its sword and missed and then simply bit her, on the shoulder, and held on.

Lilac Mist went up a tree. She did it the way a tabaxi does anything that involves claws and a trunk, in a single motion that the rest of us would call a climb and she would not call anything at all, and from the branch she had a clean line past the little gully where the wight had gone to ground. One arrow. It went straight through the thing. The wight's teeth came out of the scout's shoulder as it crumpled, and it did not get up.

Then it was mop-up, and this company mops up with enthusiasm. Stirges burst under ray and arrow, and Urida's fire bolt turned hers to ash in the air, cauterized and vaporized together in a little greasy flash. Xhosala and Josok stamped the last one flat between them, and the Feast of the Moon fell quiet in the jungle east of the Tiryki.

Grieg looked at the holes in himself and could not make much of them. Lilac could. A creature that had been feeding on undead blood, she reasoned, and then on him, might have carried anything from one to the other, and she was not going to find out the hard way. She spun, and her tail swished, and sparks of blue and violet went round the wulven where he had been bitten and sank in. It was a cleansing of the kind that drives out sickness, and whether or not he had needed it, he had it.

Josok did the same for the scout, and here the day turned.

The bite on Zamisi's shoulder closed. But the woman did not come back with it. She stayed pale. She stayed weak. Lilac Mist, who had been walking behind her for two days and knew what she had looked like that morning, saw it plainly: she was frailer than she had been, and the priest's spell, which drives out disease, had not touched whatever this was.

The whole company bent over my Guide at once, which I will confess warmed me when I heard it, and it was Urida's eye that found the passage. A wight does not simply wound. It drains the life out of what it bites, taking part of its victim's very essence. And Urida, reading, arrived at the thought that unsettled them all and has sat with them since: that in a world where the Soulmonger is turning, with the dead unable to rest and the lately raised rotting on their feet, there may be no healing that drain. Not with a priest's spell, not with a night's sleep. Not until the thing in Omu is broken.

She could not confirm it. She doubts it will heal. The company left the matter there, and drew the only conclusion that was any use to them: a wight, or anything with its touch, is a thing you kill before it reaches you, and never after.

On the first of Nightal, a day out from the tree, the mage hunter sat down with the whole company to tell them what she knew. She did it, I think, because she wanted them to live, and had buried enough of her own people to know what ignorance costs.

"Calling it a tree does not do it justice," she told them. It is several hundred feet tall. It stands above the canopy like a mountain stands above a field, and its roots may run for miles. It grew on the very ground where Rhoga's hunters ran the wizard Kolate down a century ago and the two of them, by the account of those who watched, destroyed each other in a violent explosion of negative energy. Somewhere beneath the roots lies the thing Kolate made of what he stole: the Heart of the Wild, corrupted into what the Obanashi now call the Heart of Blight.

"We have sent people before to destroy this tree," she said. "The trouble is that it costs us an enormous working of magic simply to hold the way in open." That was why she had wanted Artus: the Ring of Winter should stabilize the outer roots, and with it she believed they could keep the way open for a couple of hours, perhaps three. The roots inside are alive. The tunnels reform constantly. Most of the people she had sent down had died, she thought, not of anything with tooth or claw but simply of being lost. A handful had come back out, and they had reported that the border with the Feywild bleeds through down there, and that the roots are walked by undead, by corrupted beasts, and by strange fey creatures. What had killed the ones who did not come back is better not imagined.

Then she reached into her pack and gave Lilac Mist a stone. It was the near twin of the one Wainrath had given them in Tamalka, save that the mark on it was different. This one was tuned to the Heart of Blight, Xhosala explained. Follow its vibrations, she said, and it would lead them through whatever the tunnels became. "The stone will bring you to the heart." Her tone then softened, as if embarrassed to admit it: "There is no second stone to bring you back to the door, so go straight for the heart and nothing else. Do not linger." If the opening closed with them inside it, she would reopen it as many times as it took, but the roots would have moved by then and the company would likely never find the door. Asked how long she could give them: "Two hours. Perhaps three." And she added, tenderly: "I intend for you to live through this."

Rhoga's ghost, she added, had spoken to her people while they worked in the temple, and had told them she felt that Kolate still walked the realms. Xhosala suspects that some undead remnant of him is down there. Perhaps guarding the heart.

Last, she turned to Artus. If the Heart of the Wild were restored to its place, the Obanashi could commune with the spirits within it, and would try to dig out of them whatever could be learned of Mezro for him. Mesika, who had been listening in silence, came alight at that. "My sword is yours in this," she said. "I will keep you safe." Dragonbait, beside Artus, gave off the smell of wood smoke, and when the company looked to Artus for the meaning of it he told them: "I think he wants to go with you."

They did not argue with either offer.

They saw it long before they reached it, because it is not possible not to.

The Forsaken Tree is a twisted mass of sinuous, ash-colored wood that climbs past the canopy and keeps climbing, and the jungle for a mile around it is sick, sallow, thinned, the undergrowth dying back from the trunk as if afraid of it. The air thickens as you approach. The stench of death and decay is so heavy in the humid heat that the company found it harder to breathe with every hundred paces. And out from the trunk, for hundreds of feet in every direction, the roots rise out of the ground like a petrified wave, a frozen breaker of grey wood taller than a man in places, and in the middle of it an opening some thirty feet across, ringed by an arch of vines and branches that writhe. Slowly. Subtly. But they writhe.

Xhosala's people set about making a small camp. The scout who had been bitten sat down to do it, her body still fighting in vain against the vile bite. Artus Cimber walked up to the opening in the base of the tree and looked it over for a long moment, and then he took off his glove.

He held his bare hand out toward the vines and let the cold come off the ring into them, and the vines shrank from it, and drew back, and went still. Beside him Xhosala began her own working, the sorcery of her clan laid over the ring's cold like a second hand on the same rope.

Mustering their courage, they went in. Eight of them: Shago at the front, and Lilac Mist behind him with the stone in her hand, because the company had decided, in the dry way they decide such things, that she was their designated survivor, the one with the speed and the sense and the hardiness to get back out if everything else went wrong. Then Grieg and Vex. Then Urida and Chumble in the middle of the column where the casters belong. Then Mesika, with a khopesh on each hip, and Dragonbait, with the holy sword and his shield, at the rear. Artus stayed at the mouth with the Obanashi, bare-handed, holding the door.

Inside, the roots were moving.

Not quickly. Not the whipping of a living thing in anger. A slow, ceaseless writhing, like something turning over in its sleep, so that where four tunnels opened off the entrance when they stepped in, there were three a few minutes later, and then five. The passages ran five feet wide, sometimes ten, and sometimes they pinched down to a gap the company had to turn sideways to pass, with the roots sliding against their shoulders. The roots oozed. A thick, reddish sap ran out of them wherever they rubbed against one another, the color and the slowness of blood, and when Urida bent close to one to see if there was anything natural in it, a face formed in the wood under her nose, a human face, tormented, and sank back into the grain, and another rose a hand's breadth away and sank in its turn. She concluded that no, there was nothing natural in it.

Grieg carried the driftglobe, the company's floating light, since a wulven sees no better in the dark than a man does and neither do Shago or Mesika or the saurial. From the moment they passed the arch its light went red. Not dimmer: red, as though the roots had stained it on the way out, so that the whole company moved through that place bathed in a bloody glow, with the writhing walls on every side and the faces coming and going in them and the stench of rot so heavy that Grieg, whose nose is the sharpest in the company, could smell nothing else at all.

In Lilac's palm, the stone pulled. Gently at first, toward one tunnel rather than another, then toward a new one as the first closed. She followed it, and the company followed her.

They had not gone far when the roots opened into a wider space and three small things came out of the dark at them, running, and one of them was screaming.

It was screaming in Sylvan. Lilac Mist, who crossed once into the Feywild and brought its language back with her, understood every word, and I will spare my readers the particulars except to say that the creature was describing, with great specificity and anatomical confidence, how it meant to take each of them apart once they were dead. It wore a pointed cap of leather soaked dark with blood, and heavy iron boots that rang on the roots as it came, and it carried a blade far too large for a thing its size. A redcap. Those who own my Guide to Monsters will know the entry; Lilac Mist, I am delighted to report, had read it, and remembered it in the moment, which is more than can be said for the dragonborn, who confessed afterward that he had let the chapter slip. Behind the redcap came two meenlocks, hunched fey horrors with the heads and claws of crustaceans, that shun the light and step through shadows and put fear into any mind they get close to.

They did not get close.

Lilac marked the screaming one and put an arrow into it that would have ended a man. The redcap tore the arrow out of its own body and pointed it at her and screamed what it meant to do with it. Grieg came up with the trident under the red light, and the first thrust hit, and the second put the thing on the ground, and a third opened it again while it lay there coughing blood and still talking. And then Mesika came past them all.

She is fast. I had been told so and had not believed it: she covers ground like a cat, half again as quick as any human in the company, and she was on the redcap before it could rise, and the two khopeshes went into it three times in the space of a breath, and the stream of Sylvan stopped. That was the first time this company saw the woman from Mezro fight. They have stopped wondering whether she can.

The meenlocks came on into the light, because they had no other way to reach anyone, and the light was the end of them. In the driftglobe's glare their claws went wide of Shago and wide of the echo the wulven had set in front of himself, two swings and two misses, and they never had the darkness they needed to step out of reach. Urida's fire bolt had already taken a chunk out of one; Lilac's arrow took a far larger chunk out of the other, and the company heard it scream, a shriek that sounded like it came from every direction at once, nearly buckling their knees. Chumble's eldritch blasts finished the first. Grieg's trident finished the second, and the shrieks were silenced.

They went on, and the stone pulled, and the roots parted and closed behind them, and after a time a figure came through the wall.

Not out of a tunnel. Through the wall of the roots themselves, as if they were mist, a pale translucent shape that had been a woman once, and perhaps an elf, with the long lines of one. She saw them. She reached toward them. And Grieg, who is not the company's voice but is often the first to use it, spoke to her. "Who are you? What are you doing here?"

"Oh. Visitors." She drifted a little toward them, though not much. "I am Aviline. What brings you to this forsaken place?" Grieg told her plainly: they had come to return the Heart of Blight to its rightful owners. She did not react to that as the company had braced for. What she wanted, before anything else, was something else entirely. "I have been trapped down here so long. Tell me, tell me of the world above. Tell me what has passed on the surface. You have seen what I will never see again."

The company has met ghosts before and knows what they can do to the living. They gave her what she asked for anyway. The company's performers took the stage. Vex told her, with Lilac at his elbow filling in the beats, the story of this very chronicle: the crossing from Waterdeep, the curse that will not let the dead rest, the jungle, the temple. He drew his sword for the dramatic passages. He swished his cloak. He breathed, at the climax, a small and entirely cosmetic gout of fire, and I am told the ghost was overjoyed. It is the finest review a dragonborn noble has ever received from the dead, and he will not let anyone forget it.

"It grieves me to hear Chult so threatened," she said, "that you must fight so much." And then: "You seek the Heart of Blight. I have not seen it in some little while, but the way is easier if you go this way." She motioned toward the roots beside her, and the roots parted in her wake like a curtain drawn. The stone in Lilac's palm, which had been pulling the company down another passage altogether, swung hard toward the new one and held there. Vex thanked her for the kindness. "You are welcome," she said. "I wish you luck in your venture," she added as she dissipated.

I do not know who Aviline was. The company does not either. I know that she asked for stories, and was given one, and opened a road.

As the company moved between the roots for what felt like hours, but may have been minutes, two figures loomed ahead. They were skeletal, and they walked, and dark energy wisped off them in rags like smoke off a Shadowfell fire, eyes glowing in a menacing reddish orange. Blightwalkers, as I later learned the Obanashi call them, and the company has not met their like before. One of them turned its glowing eyes on Shago and the glow brightened, and the guide felt a surge of dark energy try to course through him and set his jaw and refused it. He took a longsword cut for his trouble, a shallow one. It was the only wound anyone in the company took under the tree all day.

Urida's fire bolt hit the other, and the fire went into its bones and ran through them, and it came apart in a flare and was gone. Not burned. Vaporized. The company stood for a moment looking at the empty place where it had been.

The first blightwalker lasted longer only because so many people wanted a piece of it, and then Shago stepped in with a spear in either hand and put both of them into it, and it was done.

And then the gloomwing.

It came out of the dark down the passage in a swoop meant to land on them before they knew it was there, and the light caught it in the air. A serpent, long as a horse, scaled in a dark that drank the red glow, with great bat's wings and eyes of smooth, semitranslucent amber. The driftglobe had robbed it of its ambush and it hung there a moment, too close and too lit, and the company fell on it as they had fallen on everything else in that tree.

Grieg's echo stepped under it and the trident took it in the air and brought it down, flat and sprawling on the roots with its wings crumpled, and once a flying thing is on the ground it is not a flying thing. Then Shago did what Shago does, three spears into it one after another, more hurt in a breath than the rest of the company had done together. Urida's spell tolled over the heap of them, a funeral bell with no bell to ring it, and the serpent shrugged off half the hurt of it: a creature so steeped in death does not much mind death's chill.

Then it got its one chance, the only one it would have, and it used it well. It heaved itself up off the roots, and it spoke a word, and the darkness came down: a globe of magical night spread over Mesika, Shago, Grieg, and Urida, so that they were suddenly blind in a blackness no driftglobe could touch. And it went for the air.

Vex, however, cannot be blinded so easily. The dragonborn fights with his eyes shut as well as open, and when the gloomwing lifted past him he put a scimitar into it on the way by. It fled down the passage into the roots, trailing darkness behind it.

Here is where the goblin's pact earns its place. Chumble's patron gave him eyes that see through any darkness, sorcerous or honest, and he walked to the edge of the black globe and looked down the passage and picked the serpent out of the tangle of roots where it had tried to hide. One eldritch blast reached it. The small fury of his kind went in behind the blast, and the gloomwing was left with a sliver of life and no will left to hold the dark together. The darkness fell apart. The whole company could see again, and could see it.

Lilac loosed twice and missed twice, which she took personally. Grieg's arrows went wide. And Mesika ran it down. Fifty feet of passage, roots underfoot, the serpent trying to drag itself clear, and the woman from Mezro covered the distance as though it were nothing and the khopeshes came down twice, and the Forsaken Tree had one fewer thing living in it.

I set down the ledger for the whole descent so far because it is remarkable: one shallow sword cut to Shago, and a little of Lilac Mist's hunting magic spent. That is all the Forsaken Tree had taken from them. It had taken, I remind you, nearly everyone else Xhosala ever sent.

The stone began to shake.

Not pull: shake, hard, against Lilac's palm, so that she had to close her fingers on it. Ahead, the tunnel pinched down to a gap so thin they went through it one at a time with the bleeding roots sliding across their faces, and then it opened, and they were at the edge of something large.

A circular chamber, wider than any space they had seen under the tree. Its walls were a solid mass of dead branches, brambles and vines, grey and black and knotted on each other to the ceiling. And in the center of it, floor to ceiling, stood a single root: one gigantic twist of wood twenty feet through, winding up out of the floor and into the dark above like a column holding the world up. In its face, at the height of a man's chest, was an opening, and in the opening sat a small reddish disc, no bigger than a coin, and tiny flecks of gold light moved across its surface.

That is the Heart of the Wild. Or what Kolate left of it, they surmised.

The company saw other things from where they stood, and I set them down as they were seen. Thick black energy, death made visible, flowing like slow water up the heaviest of the vines on the walls and into the ceiling, and down again into the great root at the center, so that the whole chamber was a circuit of death with the coin at its hub. Roots choking the way in, so that the company could advance no further than the mouth without cutting or climbing. And among the roots, moving in and out of sight, a couple of shapes the company knew too well to mistake. Zombies. Standing between them and the heart as though posted there.

And a voice. From somewhere in the dark among the roots, where none of them could see a speaker, a voice that had heard them coming. "More come to claim the heart," it said. "But its guardian shall protect it."

V.G.
silent_roll: The skin around Artus's Ring of Winter is dead, freezer-burned.

title: The Roots Fall Silent
summary:
There is a kind of villain who announces himself, and I have always been grateful to the type. A voice out of the dark that names itself the guardian of the thing you came for has told you three useful things: that the thing is worth guarding, that it is guarded, and that its keeper would sooner talk than strike first. The company took note of all three. Then Chumble Crudluck proposed a plan.

I give the plan in full, because a good deal of what follows hangs on it. The goblin would send Wickles, unseen, across the chamber to the great root. The pickle would take the coin from its hollow. The pickle would then eat the coin, be transformed by the power inside it into a thing the goblin called the "Dill Titan," lay waste to the Forsaken Tree from within, and carry the company out on its shoulders. Nobody argued for this plan. Nobody quite forbade it either. The feeling among them, as it was put to me, was that it would not be so simple, but that if by some miracle it worked they would go along with it.

The chamber, now that they had to fight in it, showed itself more plainly. The great root stood at the center with the coin in its hollow. Around it, well out toward the walls, stood four lesser roots, each as thick as a man is tall, running from floor to ceiling like the pillars of a hall. It was up these that the black energy climbed before it bent across the roof and poured down into the heart. The voice had come from behind the great root, on the side farthest from the door. Between the door and the root stood the dead.

There proved to be four of them, and they lasted about as long as it takes to say so. Lilac Mist's first arrow went wide, which she did not enjoy, and her second took the nearest so squarely that it came apart and stayed apart. The dead of Chult have an ugly habit of rising from blows that ought to finish them. None of these managed it. Mesika crossed half the chamber before anyone else had taken three steps, and the khopeshes put down the second. Chumble's blasts dropped the third, and as it fell something pale tore loose from the corpse and went streaking away to the south and west, through root and earth as though neither were there. The goblin, whose rod has its own claim on the souls of what he kills, watched it go with the look of a man who has had his pocket picked. Vex came in on the last with a scimitar in each hand and left a pile of bones.

Somewhere in the middle of this the pickle had set out.

Wickles crossed the breadth of the chamber unseen, as fast as a pickle can be made to go, and came to the hollow in the great root, and reached in. What happened next the company knows only through the goblin, who hears his familiar inside his own head. The report began well. He had it. He had it. He very nearly had it. And then: "Chumble, the roots. They are wrapped all the way around me. I cannot move. Oh, that is bad. That is the opposite of pickling. Everything is going grey and quiet, and Chumble, it is really cold in here."

There was a burst of the black energy at the mouth of the hollow, and there was no more pickle.

I ask my gentler readers not to grieve. A warlock's familiar is called back with an hour's work and a pinch of incense, and Wickles has died in these pages before. I do note, for the record, that this is not the first time something with tendrils has had hold of him, and that he is said to be forming opinions on the subject.

So much for the plan. What it had bought them was knowledge. The heart did not wish to be taken, and the roots would kill to keep it.

The guardian came out then, since nobody had come to him. He stepped from behind the great root, a man, or what a hundred years beneath that tree had left of one, and he did not waste the moment on a second speech. He threw his hand out at Mesika, the nearest of them, and the same black energy that ran in the walls went into her like water into sand, and for an instant the woman from Mezro looked as a plant looks in a drought. She set her teeth and kept her feet. He was back behind the root before anyone could answer him.

This was Kolate. A century ago he came over the sea, a wizard of Nimbral by the old accounts, and talked the high priestess Rhoga into showing him where the Heart of the Wild was kept, and stole it, and fled into the jungle with the Obanashi on his heels. They caught him on this ground. The tree is what grew of it. He named himself the heart's guardian. Whether he kept it or it kept him I could not tell you, and I am not certain he could have told you either.

Shago went after him the only way Shago goes after anything, at a dead run and shouting his own name, which is his battle cry and, I am assured, a good one. Urida had a quicker way to reach a man behind a root. She could not see him. She knew where the voice had come from, and she had the others' pointing arms, and a ball of fire does not need to be told exactly. It burst on the far side of the chamber and the company heard Kolate scream. Shago, who was nearest, saw the blood-colored sap on one of the pillars hiss and boil away under the heat, though the wood beneath never caught. And Grieg, who was watching the pillars because he had run out of zombies to watch, saw the black current in them run thicker for a moment, as though something had drawn hard upon it.

It was Vex who put steel to one first. Somebody had to. He set about the nearest pillar with both scimitars and opened it nearly halfway through in two strokes, and saw the same thing under his own blades: the more he cut, the more of the dark came flooding into the wood. Lilac Mist, from the mouth of the chamber, put two arrows into a second pillar. They stuck there and quivered, for a root minds an arrow a great deal less than it minds an edge, but that pillar darkened too, and the one Vex had been cutting did not.

Here I must give the wulven his due. Grieg is a hunter of beasts, not a scholar of the Art, and he will tell you so himself. But he stood there in the red light with his trident and thought it through, which is more than many a scholar would have done with a necromancer in the room. A pillar drank deeper when it was wounded. All of them drank deeper when Kolate was wounded. And a vessel that is filled and then broken must spill. So the pillars had to come down, since it was plainly through them that the heart was feeding its keeper, and whoever brought one down would be standing in whatever came out of it.

The company settled it in a few shouted words. Cut them nearly through. Then step back, and let the last blow fall from a distance.

Mesika opened the second pillar with three strokes and sprang clear of it. Chumble Crudluck, who had been standing very still since the hollow went quiet, found his voice. "You have hurt my pickle for the last time!" he told the chamber at large, and four rays of fire went from his hand into the farthest pillar of all, across the whole width of the dark, and every one of them struck. Then he folded himself into the roots as only a goblin can, and the chamber lost track of him entirely.

Grieg sent his echo to the pillar Mesika had opened. He put into its hand the short sword he has carried on his hip through this whole chronicle and had never once, by his own admission, drawn in anger. The echo chopped. It chopped again, and the root parted. The lower half slumped to the floor. Down the upper half the black energy came screaming, and burst, a blast no wider than a man's reach, and there was nothing within its reach but a wulven's shadow, which went out like a candle.

"Exactly as intended," said Grieg.

Kolate's answer came at once. He stepped out again, and a sickly yellow-green fog rolled out of his hands and settled over Vex, Dragonbait and Shago where they stood together by the pillar Vex had cut. Urida knew it on sight. She has never worked the spell, but every wizard has heard of the cloud that kills, and she called its name across the chamber, for whatever good a name could do them.

What did them good was the saurial. I have mentioned Dragonbait's sword in these pages and never yet had cause to describe it at work. When it is drawn, those who stand close to him bear sorcery better than they otherwise would. It is a grace of his calling. All three were standing close to him. They choked, and it burned in them, and they kept their feet.

Shago could not see his own spear. He knew which way the necromancer had gone, so he went that way, by feel, around the curve of the great root and out the far edge of the fog, and found Kolate standing directly in front of him. I am told both were surprised, and that Shago got over it first. The spear went into the wizard's shoulder to the binding.

And the tree answered.

Roots came down out of the ceiling over Kolate, reaching, as a mother snatches up a child from the road. Then they whipped back, and everything the three standing pillars had been drinking let go at once. It ran through every root in that chamber, and for all anyone can say through every root beneath the tree, and it went through the company like cold water through cloth. There was nowhere to stand that was out of it. Some of them shrugged off the worst. Vex did not, nor Dragonbait. And Urida, who is the smallest of them and wears nothing heavier than a robe, was left on her feet and very little more.

It had come through three pillars. It would have come through four if the echo had not cut one, and nobody needed the gnome to do that sum for them.

So they broke the rest, and quickly, while the roots were still spent.

Urida went first, though she had the least left to spend. Lilac Mist was calling to her to come back and be mended. The gnome's reply was to walk forward until she could see the farthest pillar, the one Chumble had scorched, and break the air around it with a clap of thunder that shook dust from the ceiling. Only then did she permit herself to be fussed over. The tabaxi came out to her at a run. The tail swished, the blue and violet sparks went round, and a good part of what the tree had taken from the gnome was given back.

Dragonbait felt his way out of the fog with one hand on the pillar Vex had been cutting, and when he could see it he took the holy sword in both fists and hit it. Light ran down the blade as it bit. It was the first time the company had seen that sword land on anything, and it took as much out of the root in a single stroke as the dragonborn's two scimitars had together. I am told there was a moment's respectful silence. He had a second stroke in him, and he held it, because Vex was standing at his elbow and the pillar was a hair from breaking. He stepped back instead.

Vex stepped back with him, well out of reach of it, and took a breath, and steadied himself, for the fog and the roots between them had cost him dearly. Then he breathed out.

My readers will recall the little gout of flame with which he closed his recital for the ghost Aviline, and which I called cosmetic. This one was not cosmetic. It took the pillar at its wounded middle and a man's height of root simply went to ash. The two ends dropped away from each other, and the black energy burst in the empty air between them and touched no one. Then the dragonborn walked out of the fog, unhurried, and took his place again at the saurial's side.

That was two. The third was the far one, scorched and thunder-struck and standing alone in the dark where only a goblin's eyes could find it. Chumble found it. One blast went wide. The second struck it square, and the pillar flew to splinters and spent its fury on an empty floor, unwitnessed, like the tree that falls in the forest in the old riddle.

That left one, the pillar on Kolate's own side of the chamber that had weathered the fireball. Grieg wanted it badly, and it was a long way round. He took the shortest line there was, close along the wall, where the lesser roots caught at his legs and tried to keep him, and he tore through them by main strength. He set his echo at the foot of the pillar and the short sword went to work again. It bit, and glanced, and Grieg dug for the burst of speed a fighter keeps in reserve for such moments, and it bit again and went through. The fourth pillar burst. The wulven lost a second shadow in as many minutes and did not appear to miss it.

With that the whole dark circuit that had so impressed the company from the doorway was broken. Nothing climbed the walls any more. Nothing poured into the heart. And there stood Kolate on the far side of the great root, with one of Shago's spears in him and nothing left at his back.

He did what he could. He turned the withering on Shago, and the guide set his jaw and took a small part of what was meant for him. Then it was Shago's turn. Kolate was quick: a shimmer of force sprang up on his arm and turned the first spear, and the second after it. It did not turn the shield. Shago put the rim of it into him with all his weight behind and laid him flat on his back among the roots, and across the chamber the yellow fog, with nobody left to mind it, thinned and went.

Urida came up on the other side and poured a cone of cold white light down the length of him, starlight by the look of it. It caught Shago's side as well, for he was standing over the man, and she called out that she was sorry, and Shago did not seem to notice he had been apologized to. Kolate noticed the light. When it faded he could see nothing farther off than the reach of a spear. And about his hands, where there had been nothing before, wisps of the black energy had begun to gather and turn.

They came at him from every quarter then. Mesika cut him once. Grieg stabbed down at him where he lay. Dragonbait was pounding around the root with the sword up. With every wound the darkness at his hands grew thicker.

I must leave them there a moment, because honesty requires me to report what Chumble Crudluck was doing while this went on.

He was at the coin. With the pillars down he had gone to the hollow in the great root to see what had killed his pickle, and found the heart shut in a little cage of rootlets, woven tight as a fist. So he took a flask of oil from his pack and emptied it over the cage, and struck a light from his tinderbox, and set it burning. The rootlets burned. They also grew, as fast as the fire could eat them, new wood pushing out through the flames. The goblin blew on it. That not sufficing, he turned his back on it and shook out the cloak the captain of the Horizon gave this company on their very first voyage, which billows grandly on command and had never until that hour been asked to do anything useful, and he fanned the fire with it. The fire roared. The roots grew. I am told it was a draw.

Meanwhile Kolate, flat on his back and all but blind, spoke a word and was not there.

Swords came down on bare roots. For a moment nobody knew where he had gone, save the two who could see the other side of the chamber. But a wulven's ears are not a man's. Grieg heard him land: a scuffle, and a weight coming to its feet against the far wall, beyond the great root. He shouted it out, and the company turned like a pack on a new scent.

Shago was off before the shout had finished, into a dark he could not see through, because that is the manner of the man. His road took him around the heart, past a goblin with his back to a fire, flapping a cloak. Chumble put out a hand for a slap of the palm as he went by. I cannot tell you whether he got one. I can tell you that Shago would have tried.

Urida's thunder found Kolate first, and he bore it. Then Lilac Mist had him. The fight had come round to her side of the chamber at last, and she laid her mark on him and loosed twice. The first arrow missed. The second he raised his shimmer against, and it went through that and through him as though neither were there. The darkness around his hands was by now blacker than anything else in that black place.

And Mesika, who had come down into the Forsaken Tree with a khopesh on each hip and no bow, and who found herself fifty feet from the enemy of her new friends with nothing to throw, did the thing a soldier does. She picked up rocks. The first two went nowhere near him. The third hit him square on the top of the head.

Chumble let the fire alone long enough to throw a larger one. It was the last great spell he had in him that day, and Kolate twisted away from the worst of it, and came out of the flames scorched and staggering and still gathering the dark to himself.

Every eye in the company could see what was building in his hands. None of them knew its name. They all knew they had come running to one place to kill him, and were now standing shoulder to shoulder around a man with one great spell left.

Grieg ran. He covered half the distance on his own legs and threw his echo the rest, and from where it stood over Kolate he struck through it with both hands on the trident. The first thrust went home. The necromancer sat up out of the roots with his hands coming together, the black energy pouring between them into a shape that was round and wide and meant for all of them. The second thrust went through both hands at once and into what lay behind them.

Urida never recognized the spell. I have described the gathering of it to others who know more of such workings than I do, and they went quiet, and asked how close together the company had been standing.

And then there was no sound at all.

Understand what that means. From the moment they had passed under the arch, the roots of that tree had been moving: turning, sliding, grinding one on another, across the better part of a mile of buried wood. They had been hearing it so long that they had stopped hearing it. When Kolate died, every root in the Forsaken Tree went still in the same instant, and the silence came down on the company like a hand. The driftglobe's light, which had burned red since the arch, paled toward its proper color. And in the hollow of the great root the little cage of rootlets, burned and regrown and burned again, uncurled like fingers and drew back, and left the coin lying in the open.

From the voice in the dark to the trident, I am told, the whole of it took about as long as it has taken you to read this page.

Nobody wanted to touch it. They remembered what had become of the last one who tried. But a company cannot stand looking at a coin forever, and it was Vex, who has never in his life let a silence go on too long, who walked up to it and gave it one cautious poke with a fingertip.

The red on the coin's face was not a color. It was spores, and they burst. A cloud of them sprayed from the hollow, and Dragonbait, who had come up close behind, took it full in the face. Shago, Urida and Vex himself caught the edges and coughed it out. The dragonborn retired several steps with what dignity he could assemble and proposed that perhaps someone better acquainted with magical devices might care to take the matter from there. He was looking at Urida.

It was the goblin who took it. Chumble dug an empty sack out of his pack, turned it inside out over his fist, and picked the Heart of Blight out of its hollow in the manner of a man tidying up after a dog. He folded the sack back over it and tied off the neck. An unseen hand, his own conjuring, patted him on the back throughout by way of encouragement. The coin did nothing further. It had spent its last defense on Vex.

As the heart left the root, the tree began to let go. All around them the roots sagged and crumbled, slowly, the way a sandbank goes, until what had been a living maze was only a warren of plain earthen tunnels. They needed no stone to find the way back. They walked out.

They had been below four hours, perhaps five. It was the middle of the afternoon when they came up into daylight, and the Obanashi were already celebrating. The arch no longer needed holding. The vines had fallen from it, and it stood open, and plainly would go on standing open. Artus Cimber sat on the ground beside it with his glove back on, grey in the face, having done nothing since morning but hold a door against a tree. Above them all the great trunk, which had been the black of old char when they went under it, was turning the dark grey-brown of ordinary bark even as they watched, and the brambles were thinning and dropping away. The tree was not dying. It had been dead for a hundred years, and it was stopping.

Xhosala came to them across the roots, and I am told she was nearer to weeping than a mage hunter likes to be seen. "Thank you. Thank you for what you have done. You have reclaimed it." And then, because she could not help herself: "Were you able to carry it out? Is it with you?"

It was with the goblin, and the goblin was off to one side with his back to everyone.

He had called Wickles back, and the pickle, restored and none the wiser, was being offered the sack. "Take it. Absorb its power," Chumble was heard to say. "You can do it. I believe in you." Wickles, I am assured, was only too happy to oblige. When holding it produced no visible result, the goblin opened the sack and stuffed the pickle in alongside the coin, and held it shut for a while. The Dill Titan did not emerge. A pickle emerged, and said it felt much the same as before.

Then Chumble Crudluck walked over and put the sack in Xhosala's hands, and her hands shook as she took it.

A hundred years the Obanashi have hunted that coin. They have buried more of their own beneath that tree than Xhosala cared to number for the company. This company went down after breakfast and brought it up before supper. I do not say it to diminish the Obanashi. I say it because I have been writing about these five for the better part of a year, and now and then one ought to step back from the banana in the dragonborn's pocket and observe what they have become.

Xhosala turned to Artus with the sack held against her chest. They would keep their word, she said. They would carry the heart back to the Seething Halls and set it in the portal where it had lain before Kolate ever came, and there were rites that would cleanse it, and when it was clean they would ask the spirits within it for whatever they held of Mezro. Mesika spoke up before Artus could. She would go with them. There was another clan that wanted the heart, as the company knew, and had spilled blood for it already, and she would see that it reached the temple.

Artus looked as though he wished to make the same offer and had to think how. He came over to the company instead. "It matters to me that they succeed in this," he said. "I know you are bound for Kir Sabal. Would you give me the time to go back to the temple with them, and meet you there a week behind?" It was five days to the Seething Halls and five days back to where they stood, he reasoned, and no call for the company to walk both. Let them go on to the aarakocra and learn what the bird-folk could offer toward the finding of Omu. "A view from the air, if they can give us one. I do not suppose they will carry us there themselves." He and Dragonbait would catch them up. Then he dropped his voice and added the other half of it: the journey would let him make certain that Mesika stayed at the temple when it was over.

The company told him to do as he liked. One of them remarked that, speaking for himself, he would not be sorry to have her along to Omu after all. She had, in fairness, shown what she could do with a rock.

It was then that the goblin asked for a word.

He asked for it in Goblin, and privately, by the little whispering cantrip he keeps for such occasions, and what he whispered was that he thought he had better go north with them. Artus did not mind. But Artus is not a fool, and he asked the obvious questions in the obvious order. Was he sure? What was going on? What had he done?

Well, said Chumble, he had given them the coin.

"What happened to Wickles, Chumble?"

"He may have absorbed whatever was inside it." And, after a moment: "They may be holding a plain, ordinary coin."

I set down the goblin's reasoning as he gave it. The pickle did not feel any different, not yet, but who could say how long that would last? He thought Wickles might need an exorcism. He would not send him away and call him back, as a warlock ordinarily may, for fear that sending him away would loose whatever was now inside him. He proposed to treat the matter as one treats a deadly poison, which travels faster through an excited body, and to that end he had fitted the pickle with a falconer's hood, the little leather cap that keeps a hawk quiet on the fist, and told him to sit still and think of nothing. And he had decided that the Obanashi should be left to believe they carried the Heart of the Wild. They would at least be careful with it.

I report this without comment, save one. I have no idea whether he is right. Neither has he. I print it in the confidence that the Obanashi are not among my subscribers.

So the company divided. North, toward the Seething Halls, went Xhosala and her five, with the sack; and Mesika, guarding it; and Artus Cimber and Dragonbait; and Chumble Crudluck, with a hooded pickle riding very still upon his shoulder. The parting was brief. "It has been real, and it has been fun," the goblin told Grieg, "but it has not been real fun." The wulven wished him joy of his pickle. "Do not die," he added. "I do not much care whether the pickle does." This was unkind, and I am told it landed, for Wickles had been warming to Grieg ever since the wulven stitched him a poncho some months back.

The rest made camp where they stood, in the shadow of a tree that was slowly remembering how to be one.

* * *

In the morning there were five of them: Grieg, Vex, Urida, Lilac Mist, and Shago to show the way. They turned southwest. Artus had told them of a gorge in that country, Ataaz Muhahah, the Laughing Gorge, and of the ancient span of stone that crosses it, which would save them days on the road to Kir Sabal.

They had not been walking long when Lilac Mist and Grieg both stopped and looked left. Thirty feet off the trail, under a hundred years of moss and creeper, something stood that the jungle had not made. They pulled the green away from it. It was a statue, ten feet tall: a king of Chult, done in the old stiff manner, crowned and robed for some high occasion and staring over their heads into the trees.

They asked Shago who it was, he being the only one among them born in this land. He studied it for a good while. He did not know. The merchant princes have ruled for as long as he can remember, he said, and this was none of them. Some leader out of the old days, important enough that somebody had cut his likeness in stone and carried it out here. As to its age, none of them is a mason, and the best they could make of the weathering was a hundred years at the least, give or take, as one of them put it, a hundred years.

Somebody had loved it once. There was tribute heaped at its feet, or the ghost of tribute: fruit long gone to black earth, the stems of flowers, things that had rotted to nothing in the rains. One offering had lasted. Lilac turned it up out of the mold, and Grieg, looking over her shoulder, knew it the moment she did.

Readers with long memories will know it too. It was an iron token, the twin of the one Shago carries in his own pouch: the mark he showed the company in Port Nyanzaru, when they brought him word that there was a writ out on his life, and that he called a mistake. This one was older, and pitted by the weather. It was otherwise the same in every particular, down to the lettering.

Nobody had ever read the lettering. Vex could. There is a gift that comes with the banner he fights under, and it lets him take the sense of any writing if he studies it long enough, whether or not he knows the tongue. He did not know this one. He turned the token in his fingers for some time, and then he read it out, feeling his way around a word that meant nothing to him.

"Ytepka Society."

He had never heard it. None of them had. Shago had never heard it spoken either. But he looked at the word for a long moment, and said slowly that it was an odd one, and that he thought he had seen it before, written down, on papers at home.

That is all they learned, and they are on a clock that does not allow for turning back to Port Nyanzaru to ask. So I leave it as they left it. A token that means death, laid as an offering at the feet of a forgotten king. I have my own notions about that word. They belong to a later chapter of this chronicle, and the reader shall have them there, when the company has earned theirs.

The day after was the fourth of Nightal, and nothing troubled it until dark. With the party so reduced they made new watches: Lilac Mist and Vex for the first, and Grieg, Shago and Urida for the second. The three lay down under the gnome's little dome. The two sat by a low fire, with the driftglobe dark so as to draw no eyes.

The first watch was hardly begun when something came running out of the jungle at them.

It was a tree. It was, to be exact, about a foot of tree: a sapling, up on its roots and running on them, rustling for all it was worth. It did not attack. It stopped short of the fire and shook itself at them, every leaf going, with the frantic purpose of a dog that needs you to follow it this instant.

Three days before, the company had gone down among roots that wanted them dead. Lilac Mist looked at this one and did the courteous thing. She greeted it in Sylvan, the tongue of the fey, and asked how they might help it.

The sapling stopped shaking. It tipped itself to one side, the way a dog cocks its head at a word it almost knows.

Then it answered her. It had not come for help. It had come with a warning, and it gave the warning and pointed, with what it had for an arm, into the dark to the south.

"You have undead coming your way."

V.G.
